title: What a Debate Is
summary: A debate is a contest of reasons with rules: two sides, one question, fair turns, and a judge who decides which side argued better, not which side is right.

p: In a debate, two sides take turns giving reasons about one question. One side argues for it, the other against. A judge (or an audience) listens to both and decides which side made the better case in that round.

That last part matters. A debate doesn't settle whether school uniforms are good. It settles which team argued better about school uniforms on Tuesday afternoon. That is why debaters can argue a side they don't personally hold, and why the same topic can be won by either side.

sections.h: How it differs from an argument
p: An everyday argument and a debate both involve disagreeing, but a debate adds rules that make it fair and useful.

rows: Equal, timed speeches in a set order
Usually no one; sometimes whoever gives up last
A judge decides, and explains why
Sources you can name and the other side can check
To make the best case and test the other one

list: **The resolution**: the statement being debated, such as "Resolved: Schools should start no earlier than 8:30 a.m." (See [Reading a Resolution](/debate/learn/resolutions/).)
**Two sides**: the **affirmative** (or pro, or proposition, or government) supports the resolution; the **negative** (or con, or opposition) opposes it.
**Speeches**: **constructives** build a case; **rebuttals** answer the other side and sum up.
**Questioning**: most formats give each side time to question the other: **cross-examination**, **crossfire**, or **points of information**.
**Prep time**: a few minutes each side can use between speeches to plan.
**A judge**: who fills out a **ballot** with the winner and the reason for the decision.

p: Debaters learn to research a question, organize their thoughts, speak in front of others, listen closely, and think on their feet. Just as important, they learn to understand views they don't share. You can't answer an argument you don't understand, so debate trains you to listen for the best version of the other side.

Aristotle, writing more than two thousand years ago, put it this way: we should be able to argue on opposite sides of a question, not so we can argue for what is wrong, but so we "see clearly what the facts are" and can answer someone who argues unfairly.

example.title: A two-minute practice round at the dinner table. Resolution: Our family should have pizza night every Friday.

lines.s: Pizza night gives us one dinner a week nobody has to cook, so whoever usually cooks gets a break. It's also something to look forward to at the end of the week.

A break for the cook is a good goal, but takeout pizza every week costs a lot over a year, and it's the same meal every time. A rotating Friday where a different person cooks something simple gives the break without the cost.
They agree the cook needs a break. Their plan still makes someone cook. Ours is the only one where nobody does. We can keep the cost down by making pizza at home from frozen dough.
If we're making it at home, someone is cooking after all. So the real question is which costs less and gives more variety, and that's the rotating Friday.

example.note: Notice what both sides did: each answered the other side's actual point, agreed where it was fair to agree, and ended by telling the judge what the round comes down to.

p: Most American high schools with a team compete in leagues run by the National Speech & Debate Association or a state association. Homeschoolers have leagues of their own (NCFCA and Stoa), and many colleges have teams. You don't need a league to start: a classroom, a co-op or a family can hold debates with a timer and a topic. See [Formats](/debate/formats/) and [Resources](/debate/resources/).

practice: Pick a topic from the [topics list](/debate/topics/) and write one sentence for each side.
Hold the two-minute dinner-table debate above with a family member, then switch sides and do it again.
Watch a short recorded debate and write down the resolution, the two sides and who you think won, with one reason.
